no_intervention_scenario.summary: If nobody acts for 5–10 years, the everyday Lebanese dialect as a whole will almost certainly survive, because it is the default language of media, politics and online chat. What erodes is narrower and harder to replace: unstable magnetic tapes in under-funded broadcasters and private homes; regional and older registers that are giving way to a media-driven Beirut-centred koine; oral genres tied to village gatherings; the contextual knowledge (who, where, when) held by retiring archive staff and elders; and family transmission in a diaspora that keeps growing. Meanwhile, publicly posted Lebanese speech keeps being harvested by large companies on terms that communities do not control.
what_is_lost: Undigitised tapes held by private, regional and defunct radio and TV stations, and recordings made at home
Regional phonology, vocabulary and older registers spoken by elderly rural speakers
Context metadata about archive items once knowledgeable staff and elders are gone
The community's bargaining position over how its voice data is used, once that data has been scraped
what_value_remains: A partly digitised and inventoried public broadcaster archive (Télé Liban, Radio Liban, the National News Agency)
Private sound archives such as AMAR's early-recording collections
Zajal's UNESCO inscription and its place on the national register of intangible heritage
Many living speakers, at home and abroad, plus a vast volume of informal online dialect (Arabizi, Arabic script, video)
Legal hooks already in force: Law 75/1999 limits broadcaster rights to 50 years from broadcast, and Law 81/2018 exempts personal and household processing

faces_found.what_it_requires: Broadcasters hold related rights for 50 years from broadcast and performers for 50 years from performance. Works inspired by folklore are protected. There is no general fair-use clause, only specific exceptions. Clearance is therefore needed for anything less than 50 years old.

faces_found.face: Lebanese law as written: personal data (Law 81/2018)
faces_found.what_it_requires: Personal data processing must have a legal basis. The law has no category for sensitive data, no independent authority, and exempts purely personal or household processing.

faces_found.face: EU GDPR imposed by foreign funders
faces_found.what_it_requires: Voice processed to identify a speaker is special-category data, prohibited by default unless an exception applies, such as explicit consent. Funders also expect minimisation, storage limits, documented legal bases and data-subject rights, which is stricter than Lebanese law.
In practice, nothing protects publicly posted speech from being used to train models. Only access control, licence terms and hosting choices actually limit reuse.

faces_found.face: Broadcaster and state ownership of archives
faces_found.what_it_requires: The public archives sit under the Ministry of Information, so access depends on ministerial and institutional agreement and on political continuity. Private broadcasters decide for themselves.
Speakers, families and localities expect a say over how their voices are used. This norm is not codified in Lebanon but drives trust; compare the Māori data-sovereignty licences.
Safeguarding must be community-led, based on consent, and aimed at keeping a practice alive, not freezing it in an archive.
War, displacement and power cuts make copies held in a single location unsafe. Off-site redundancy and emergency protocols are needed.
Writing norms favour Standard Arabic, so access designed around text excludes non-readers and those who write only in Arabizi. Oral and audio channels need to be designed in from the start.

options.name: Rights-triage register for broadcaster archives
options.description: Reframe the bottleneck as legal uncertainty rather than technology. Sort every archive item into one of four buckets: over 50 years since broadcast; broadcaster-owned and under 50 years; contains performers or third-party works; unknown. Publish the register so that funders and users can act on the items that are already clear.
actors: Télé Liban and Radio Liban archive units
who_could_be_left_out: heirs of performers who are not consulted
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Broadcasters treat the register as a liability disclosure and refuse to cooperate, or ministerial turnover stalls the work.

options.name: Rescue tapes at private and regional stations
options.description: Survey private TV channels, regional and defunct radio stations, and their retired technicians for surviving tapes. Offer free transfer in exchange for a preservation copy and a basic rights agreement. Give priority to formats at physical risk.
who_benefits: regional communities whose local radio was never archived
who_could_be_left_out: stations that have already closed with no successor holding rights
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Owners fear losing commercial value, or tapes have already been recycled or discarded.

options.name: Household off-air recording amnesty
options.description: Invite families to bring old VHS tapes, cassettes and reel recordings made from TV and radio, or of family gatherings, to mobile digitisation days. The family keeps the original and a copy. With consent, the archive keeps a copy for gaps in broadcaster holdings.
who_benefits: older people who hold the media
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Families fear that their private recordings will be exposed, or broadcasters object to copies of their programmes being kept.

support.claim: Home recordings may fill gaps where broadcasters overwrote their own tapes.

options.name: Re-broadcast archives on free airwaves
options.description: Instead of putting the archive online first, schedule rights-cleared archive programmes on terrestrial TV and radio. Broadcast reaches older, low-income and rural audiences without internet access or literacy, and it is harder to scrape in bulk.
who_could_be_left_out: younger audiences who do not watch linear TV
options.what_would_make_it_fail: The public broadcaster lacks funds or a reliable power supply, or performer rights block re-broadcast.

support.claim: The public broadcaster was the only channel for decades, so its archive is shared memory.

options.name: Phone line to listen to archives
options.description: Set up a free or low-cost phone number with a keypad menu (by region, genre or decade) that plays short archive excerpts and lets callers leave a spoken comment or memory. It works on any basic phone and needs no reading.
who_benefits: people who do not read or write
who_could_be_left_out: people who cannot afford call costs if the line is not free
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Call costs, the operator's unwillingness to zero-rate the line, or no budget to curate the excerpts.

options.name: Schoolchildren interview their elders
options.description: Model a scheme on Ireland's 1937 Schools' Collection: pupils record elders at home on a shared list of themes (sayings, work songs, games, remedies, place names). The pupil, family and school keep copies. Families may deposit them with an archive if they consent.
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Teacher overload and strikes, privacy fears, or sectarian sensitivities over some themes.

support.claim: Ireland used schoolchildren as folklore collectors at national scale.
support.fragment: embarked on a project with an unlikely group of researchers: schoolchildren

options.name: Diaspora volunteers transcribe and tag recordings
options.description: Run an online platform where volunteers anywhere transcribe and tag archive audio, in Arabic script or in an agreed Arabizi convention, and add place and context notes. This turns diaspora nostalgia into catalogue work.
who_benefits: future users who search by text
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Inconsistent spelling, low volunteer retention, or rights holders refusing online exposure.

support.claim: Ireland's folklore collection was transcribed by crowdsourcing.
support.fragment: online crowdsourcing effort to digitize and transcribe

support.claim: There are local efforts to standardise a written form of Lebanese.

options.name: Community guardianship licence for voice collections
options.description: Adapt the Māori Kaitiakitanga licence model: speakers grant use for community benefit and education only, and surveillance or unconsented commercial training is excluded. A trusted custodian holds the data as a guardian, not as an owner.
who_could_be_left_out: groups without a recognised representative body
commercial users who would build public tools
options.what_would_make_it_fail: There is no single legitimate community body in a plural society, or the licence cannot be enforced against foreign actors.

support.claim: The licence keeps control of the data with the community.
support.fragment: ensures that data sovereignty remains within local communities

support.claim: Speakers should have a say over secondary uses of their voices.

options.name: Consent-only speech recognition to index archives
options.description: Train a small speech-recognition model only on consented Lebanese speech, and use it to generate searchable transcripts of archive hours that humans could never transcribe by hand. The model stays under the custodian's licence and is not released for open reuse.
who_could_be_left_out: speakers of under-represented regional varieties, who may be transcribed badly
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Too little consented data, poor accuracy on regional varieties, or pressure to release or sell the model.

support.claim: A broadcaster-led model trained only on consented data is feasible.
support.fragment: built exclusively from material contributed with full consent

options.name: Shield archives from bulk harvesting
options.description: Reframe the archive as an asset that can be extracted. Serve audio by streaming only, with tiered access (public excerpts, registered full access, research agreements), explicit no-training terms, and self-hosting instead of large platforms. Bulk access is negotiated, not scraped.
who_could_be_left_out: casual users who face sign-up friction
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Determined scrapers bypass the controls, or the friction kills public use.

options.name: Legal reform for heritage archives
options.description: Propose amendments to Law 75/1999: a preservation copy exception for archives, an orphan-works regime for recordings whose rights holders cannot be traced, and a clear rule for folklore-based recordings. This removes legal fog for every actor at once.
who_could_be_left_out: communities if folklore rules favour the state
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Parliamentary paralysis, and lobbying by rights holders.

support.claim: Folklore-inspired works are protected, which complicates reuse of heritage recordings.
support.fragment: However, works inspired by folklore shall enjoy protection.

options.name: Single consent protocol meeting both legal regimes
options.description: Write one plain-language, oral-first consent protocol that satisfies both GDPR (explicit, granular, revocable consent; no speaker identification unless agreed) and Lebanese law, so that foreign-funded projects do not each improvise. It includes a version read aloud for non-readers.
who_could_be_left_out: people who cannot consent (deceased speakers in old recordings)
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Funders' lawyers reject a shared template, or the protocol becomes too heavy for fieldwork.
